extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humour studies, philosophy of mind, and intellectual history
extracted.subtask_description: Critical reading and comparison of historical/theoretical accounts of laughter (incongruity, superiority, relief), with attention to physiological, moral, and historical/contextual claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examples in philosophical exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Schopenhauer conceded that examples are necessary 'in order to come to the assistance of the mental inertness of those readers who prefer always to remain in a passive condition' (ibid.: 55).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete examples to illustrate abstract claims so readers can grasp concepts. However, avoid insulting or alienating readers; testing examples with representative audiences ('Wise Club' thought-experiment) can reveal whether an example misfires. Anti-pattern: choosing examples that reveal the moral blind spots of the theorist (e.g., Schopenhauer's insensitive epitaph example) — such examples may illustrate the theory but undermine its acceptability and universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity as basis for laughter (Schopenhauer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Schopenhauer's account: laughter arises from perceiving an incongruity (illustrated by the line tangent to a circle appearing angular on paper), which 'will easily excite a smile' (ibid.: 55).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a theoretical claim, incongruity should identify the perceived mismatch that triggers mirth. But beware overgeneralizing: the existence of an incongruity does not guarantee laughter — cultural, moral, and situational factors modulate response. Example: the circle/tangent image may be amusing in some contexts but not universally so; theoretical accounts should not assume universal audience reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral taste and target-sensitivity in humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception of incongruity is not sufficient for laughter; moral blindness or a hardened heart can determine whether a given incongruity elicits mirth (Schopenhauer's racist epitaph example shows that laughter can be morally objectionable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate humour not only by formal perceptual features (incongruity) but also by the moral status of the target and the audience's ethical sensibilities. Anti-pattern: treating an 'everybody' who laughs as truly universal and neglecting the perspectives of those directly affected (e.g., grieving individuals). Theorists should acknowledge that some instances of perceived incongruity are ethically problematic and may indicate cruelty rather than innocent humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between wit and folly
rubrics_metrics.description: Schopenhauer: 'With wit, a person intentionally brings together two distinct objects under the same concept, but with folly, a person is led by a concept to treat two obviously distinct objects as if they were actually similar' (ibid.: 53).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing jokes or utterances, classify whether the humor stems from a deliberate conceptual juxtaposition (wit) or from a conceptual mistake that makes the speaker appear foolish (folly). Use this distinction to explain whether laughter is directed at cleverness or at the speaker's error; it helps to diagnose comedic intent versus social sanctioning of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical testability: account must explain non-laughter cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Bain's critique of incongruity: many incongruities (e.g., 'a decrepit man under a heavy burden, five loaves and two fishes among a multitude ... an instrument out of tune, a fly in ointment, snow in May') do not provoke laughter (1865 edn: 247–8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satisfactory theory of humour must predict not only when laughter occurs but also when it does not. Use counterexamples to falsify or refine general claims (incongruity alone is insufficient). Empirical or observational checks are necessary: assemble catalogues of incongruous situations that fail to evoke mirth and explain why (moral gravity, pity, disgust, contextual factors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief theory: laughter as release of nervous energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Relief theory (Bain, Spencer): laughter acts to relieve pressure by discharging nervous energy; Bain linked pleasure with an 'increase of the vital functions' and laughter to a 'heightening of the powers of life' (1868a edn: 283; 291).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying relief theory, identify the source of accumulated excitation and the mechanism by which laughter dispels it. Consider physiological correlates and whether the laughter observed corresponds to energy release rather than purely cognitive appraisal. Scoring note: relief accounts may be stronger when supported by physiological description or experimental evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological grounding: nervous system as receiver/distributor of energy (Spencer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spencer: the nervous system 'functions to receive and transmit energy' and operates 'as a liberator of motion' and 'as a distributor or apportioner of the motion liberated' (1881, vol. I: 47–49).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorists invoking physiology should specify mechanisms (what is received, how excitation diffuses, which muscular/visceral responses follow). Avoid vague key terms; link claims to contemporary physiological concepts where possible. Use anatomical/functional detail to ground claims about laughter's bodily manifestations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Diffusion and unconscious processes (Bain, Carpenter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bain's Law of Diffusion: 'the greater the initial stimulation, the greater will be the diffusion' (Bain, 1865: 6–7). Carpenter's 'unconscious cerebration': much neurological processing occurs below conscious awareness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate how excitation spreads through the organism and how unconscious dynamics (habits, reflexes, unconscious cerebration) contribute to laughter. Theorists should account for automatic muscular/visceral reactions and how they interplay with conscious appraisal. Anti-pattern: attributing all laughter to conscious cognitive recognition without acknowledging unconscious diffusion and reflexive elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theories bear the imprint of their philosophy and historical context
rubrics_metrics.description: Dugas (1902): 'every theory of laughter bears the imprint of a philosophy'; the chapter shows how relief and incongruity theories reflect nineteenth-century materialism, physiology, Darwinian thought, and their authors' social backgrounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or constructing theories of humour, situate them historically and philosophically: identify underlying metaphysical commitments, disciplinary influences (e.g., physiology, evolutionary theory), and social/political positions of theorists. Use this context to explain emphases, blind spots, or biases in the theory (e.g., Spencer's evolutionary systems framing vs. eighteenth-century aesthetics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrative requirement: theories should relate humour to seriousness and broader systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory must 'make sense of seriousness' as well as predict laughter; Spencer aimed to show laughter as an illustration of broader principles of development across biological, social, and physical systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A robust theory explains how humour fits into larger accounts of mind, society, or biology (not merely isolated predictions about mirth). Evaluate whether a theory coherently integrates humour with emotions, social function, evolutionary role, or systemic principles (e.g., Spencer's systems/evolutionary project). Theories that merely catalogue triggers without connecting to broader functions are limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and verbosity as indicators of theoretical stance
rubrics_metrics.description: The physical solidity and tone of nineteenth-century treatises (massive cloth-backed volumes, heavily revised editions) reflect the earnest, system-building ambitions of their authors (Spencer, Bain) and thus their approach to humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read authors' stylistic choices (length, tone, examples, level of physiological detail) as part of the theory: dense, systematizing prose may signal ambition to subsume humour into grand theory, while concise literary treatises may prioritize aesthetic or rhetorical aspects. Use this to temper expectations about scope and claims.
